### ☐ `fact.music.sound_compressions`: unverified

> **Claim:** A vibrating object pushes on the air, making compressions (high pressure) and rarefactions (low pressure) that travel outward as a pressure wave.

- **Concept:** Sound is vibration (`concept.music.sound_vibration`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L2 “What Sound Is” · `card.music.002.c2` (text): Sound is a squeeze, passed along / A plucked string swings back and forth, shoving the air beside it. Each shove squeezes the air together (a compression), and each swing back leaves it thinner (a rarefaction). Those squeezes travel outward as a pressure wave. The air itself doesn't fly across the room to you. Its molecules jiggle back and forth in place and hand the push along, like a squeeze running down a Slinky.
  - L2 “What Sound Is” · `card.music.002.c4` (text): The last step happens in you / When the wave reaches you, it pushes on your eardrum, and your eardrum vibrates along with it, passing the motion to three tiny bones in your middle ear. So every song you've ever heard arrived the same way: as air pressing on a thin membrane, again and again. Music, underneath everything, is organized air pressure.
  - L3 “Pitch” · `card.music.003.c2` (text): Pitch is how fast the air shakes / Remember Level 2's string, squeezing the air? How many times per second it vibrates is its frequency, counted in hertz (Hz). Your ear hears frequency as pitch: faster vibrations sound higher, slower ones lower. So that standard A is the air being squeezed and released 440 times every second. High and low, in music, really means fast and slow.
  - L10 “Checkpoint: How Music Works” · `card.music.010.c2` (timeline): One A, from page to ear: On the page: Second space of the treble staff: the A above middle C; Played: A string vibrates 440 times a second; In the air: Compressions and rarefactions travel about 343 m/s; At the ear: The eardrum vibrates along with them; In the cochlea: Hair cells in one spot respond to that pitch
  - L10 “Checkpoint: How Music Works” · `card.music.010.c4` (text): The whole chapter in one breath / Sound is air pressure, shaking. Pitch is how fast it shakes. Rhythm is when the sounds start and stop over a steady beat; melody is single notes strung into one line; harmony is notes sounding at the same time. Everything else in this chapter, from triads to octaves to the staff, is a way of organizing those shakes.
  - L11 “Families of Instruments” · `card.music.011.c2` (text): Ask one question: what vibrates? / Remember Level 2: every sound starts with something vibrating and pushing on the air. In 1914, Erich von Hornbostel and Curt Sachs built a way to sort the world's instruments on exactly that. Forget what an instrument is made of or where it comes from. Ask only what vibrates first to make the sound.
  - L15 “Percussion” · `card.music.015.c2` (text): A skin, or the whole thing / Use Level 11's rule. In percussion, two answers come up. On a drum, a stretched membrane vibrates: a membranophone. On a bell, a clapper or a rattle, the instrument's own body vibrates: an idiophone. Either way, the hit only starts things; the shaking surface does the work, pushing on the air like any other vibrating object.
  - L71 “Recorded Sound” · `card.music.071.c3` (text): Playback is recording run in reverse / Remember Level 2: sound is a pressure wave, squeezes and thinnings of the air. The pits in the foil were a frozen copy of that pattern. To play it back, a lighter stylus traced the same pits and shook a second diaphragm, which pushed the air into the same squeezes all over again. Vibration became dents, and dents became vibration. The only motor was your hand on the crank.
- **Tested by:**
  - L2 `question.music.002.q2`: A speaker plays across a room. What do the air molecules between you and it do? → **Jiggle back and forth, passing the push along**
  - L10 `question.music.010.q3`: On this chapter's page-to-ear trip, what physically carries the A from the string to you? → **Compressions and rarefactions in the air**
  - L71 `question.music.071.q3`: Using Level 2's idea of sound, what were the pits in Edison's tinfoil really a copy of? → **The pattern of pressure squeezes in the sound wave**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. OpenStax and Britannica each describe sound waves in air as alternating compressions and rarefactions moving out from the source. Sources: https://www.britannica.com/science/sound-physics, https://openstax.org/books/college-physics-2e/pages/17-1-sound

### ☐ `fact.music.pitch_is_frequency`: unverified

> **Claim:** Pitch is how we perceive frequency: a sound is higher or lower according to how many times per second its source vibrates, measured in hertz (Hz).

- **Concept:** Pitch is frequency (`concept.music.pitch_frequency`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L3 “Pitch” · `card.music.003.c2` (text): Pitch is how fast the air shakes / Remember Level 2's string, squeezing the air? How many times per second it vibrates is its frequency, counted in hertz (Hz). Your ear hears frequency as pitch: faster vibrations sound higher, slower ones lower. So that standard A is the air being squeezed and released 440 times every second. High and low, in music, really means fast and slow.
  - L8 “Scales and Octaves” · `card.music.008.c2` (text): Up an octave: double it / Pitch is frequency, as Level 3 showed, and an octave up means exactly twice the frequency. From the tuning A at 440 Hz you climb to 880 Hz; go down an octave and you reach 220 Hz. That's why note letters run A to G and then start again at A. The octave travels well, too: it's a constant in the scales of most of the world's musical cultures.
  - L10 “Checkpoint: How Music Works” · `card.music.010.c4` (text): The whole chapter in one breath / Sound is air pressure, shaking. Pitch is how fast it shakes. Rhythm is when the sounds start and stop over a steady beat; melody is single notes strung into one line; harmony is notes sounding at the same time. Everything else in this chapter, from triads to octaves to the staff, is a way of organizing those shakes.
  - L74 “The Electric Guitar” · `card.music.074.c3` (text): How a magnet hears a string / Here's the physics. A steel string vibrating near the magnet changes the magnetic field running through the coil, and by Faraday's law that change pushes a small voltage through the wire. The voltage wiggles at the string's own frequency. Remember Level 3: pitch is frequency. So the note survives the trip into electricity, and an amplifier then makes the signal louder and sends it out through a speaker.
  - L84 “Synthesizers” · `card.music.084.c2` (text): The oscillator sets the pitch / An oscillator makes a repeating electrical wave. Remember Level 3: pitch is frequency, how many times per second something vibrates. On Robert Moog's synthesizer, pressing a key sent the oscillator a voltage that depended on which key you pressed, and that set the pitch. Some wave shapes are rich: a sawtooth wave contains all the harmonics of its note, higher frequencies stacked on top. That gives the next step something to carve.

### ☐ `fact.music.eguitar_pickup_induction`: unverified

> **Claim:** A magnetic pickup works by Faraday's law: a vibrating steel string changes the magnetic field through a coil, inducing a voltage that vibrates at the string's own frequency.

- **Concept:** How an electric guitar pickup works (`concept.music.eguitar_pickup`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L74 “The Electric Guitar” · `card.music.074.c3` (text): How a magnet hears a string / Here's the physics. A steel string vibrating near the magnet changes the magnetic field running through the coil, and by Faraday's law that change pushes a small voltage through the wire. The voltage wiggles at the string's own frequency. Remember Level 3: pitch is frequency. So the note survives the trip into electricity, and an amplifier then makes the signal louder and sends it out through a speaker.
  - L80 “Checkpoint: Rock and Pop” · `card.music.080.c4` (text): The chapter in one breath / Edison's phonograph let sound be stored and played back. Radio sent one performance into millions of homes at once. Rock and roll merged rhythm and blues with country, led by Black pioneers. The electric guitar's pickup turned vibrating strings into a signal an amplifier could make loud. And MTV made how a song looked as important as how it sounded. Each new machine changed who could hear music, and how.
- **Tested by:**
  - L74 `question.music.074.q1`: What does an electric guitar's pickup do? → **Turns the strings' vibrations into an electrical signal**
  - L74 `question.music.074.q3`: A guitar string vibrates 440 times a second over a pickup. Using Level 3's pitch, what does the signal do? → **Wiggles 440 times a second, so the note stays an A**
  - L77 `question.music.077.q3`: Hendrix's rockets and sirens came from an electric guitar. From Level 74, how does its sound get that big? → **A pickup makes a signal, and an amplifier boosts it to a speaker**
  - L80 `question.music.080.q5`: From Level 74's electric guitar physics: what does a vibrating steel string change inside a pickup? → **The magnetic field through a coil of wire**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. A University of Delaware physics lab and Horton and Moore's model of the pickup explain the induced voltage from a moving steel string by Faraday's law. Sources: https://www.physics.udel.edu/~nowak/phys208/Labs/FaradayLaw.pdf, https://scholarship.rollins.edu/stud_fac/14/

- **Source:** `source.sciencedaily_mcgill_music_chills_2011`
- **URL:** https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2011/01/110112111117.htm

### ☐ `fact.music.brain_dopamine_peak_chills`: unverified

> **Claim:** A 2011 brain-imaging study found dopamine released in the striatum at peak moments of pleasurable music that gave listeners chills.

- **Concept:** Music and the reward chemical (`concept.music.brain_music_dopamine`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L91 “Music and the Brain” · `card.music.091.c1` (text): Your favorite song and a good meal share a brain chemical. / When a piece of music gives you chills, your brain releases dopamine, a chemical also involved in the pleasure of rewards like food. Scientists caught it happening in 2011. But before a song can thrill you, it has to get into your head at all. Let's follow it in.
  - L91 “Music and the Brain” · `card.music.091.c4` (text): The chills are chemistry / Back to the hook. In that 2011 study, music that gave listeners chills released dopamine in the striatum, deep in the brain. The timing was the surprise. At the peak moment, the release centered on one region, the nucleus accumbens. In the run-up, while listeners anticipated the peak, it came from another, the caudate. Your brain pays out twice: once for the big moment, and once for the wait.
  - L93 “Music and Emotion” · `card.music.093.c5` (fact): Some people with normal hearing get little pleasure from music. / A 2014 study described healthy people who heard music normally but got little pleasure from it, and their bodies showed no response to music others loved. - **Tested by:**
  - L91 `question.music.091.q1`: In the 2011 brain-scan study of musical chills, which chemical was released at the peak moments? → **Dopamine**

### ☐ `fact.music.pythagoras_ratios`: unverified

> **Claim:** Greek tradition credits Pythagoras, a 6th-century-BCE philosopher, with finding that the octave, fifth and fourth match the ratios 2:1, 3:2 and 4:3, seen in string lengths.

- **Concept:** Pythagoras and musical ratios (`concept.music.pythagorean_ratios`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L22 “Music in Ancient Greece” · `card.music.022.c1` (text): Pluck a string, then pluck half of it. Same note, only higher. / At the same tension, the half-length string vibrates twice as fast, and you hear the octave. Greek tradition says Pythagoras found the numbers hiding behind sounds like this. Then Greek thinkers went further and argued that music could shape who you become.
  - L22 “Music in Ancient Greece” · `card.music.022.c2` (text): Harmony by the numbers / Greek tradition credits Pythagoras, a 6th-century-BCE philosopher, with finding that the sweetest intervals match simple ratios of string length. Halve a string (2:1) and you get the octave. Take two-thirds of it (3:2) for a fifth, three-quarters (4:3) for a fourth. Remember Level 8's A climbing from 440 to 880 Hz? That's the same 2:1, seen from the frequency side: half the length, double the vibrations.
  - L27 “Polyphony” · `card.music.027.c3` (text): Organum: chant plus a shadow / The earliest written polyphony is organum, described in Musica enchiriadis (c. 900): a voice added to a chant, the two moving note against note. Often the added voice simply doubled the chant a fourth or a fifth below. Remember Level 22's Greek ratios? The fourth (4:3) and the fifth (3:2) were the Greeks' concords too.
  - L23 “Music in Ancient China and India” · `card.music.023.c2` (text): One bell, two notes / The Zeng bells, from Suizhou in Hubei province, are the largest and best-preserved set of bronze bells in the world. They follow a 'one bell, two tones' system: each sounds two notes, depending on where it's struck. And they carry 3,755 characters of inscriptions about music theory, the earliest surviving archaeological documents to show mathematical relationships in music. Remember Level 22's ratios? China was doing the math too, in bronze.
- **Tested by:**
  - L22 `question.music.022.q1`: In the Greek ratios credited to Pythagoras, which string-length ratio gives the octave? → **2:1**
  - L22 `question.music.022.q3`: A string's 2:1 length ratio gives an octave. How does that match Level 8's A at 440 Hz and 880 Hz? → **Half the length gives double the frequency**
  - L23 `question.music.023.q3`: What do the Zeng bell inscriptions share with the Greek ratios of Level 22? → **Both link musical notes to mathematics**
  - L27 `question.music.027.q3`: Early organum often doubled the chant a fourth or a fifth below. What links those intervals to Level 22? → **They're the Greek concords 4:3 and 3:2**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Britannica's Western music article says Pythagoras was the first to record the vibratory ratios behind the Western series of notes; the Pythagorean hammers article gives 2:1, 3:2 and 4:3 for octave, fifth and fourth.   - L52 “Indian Classical Music” · `card.music.052.c3` (text): Tala: time that comes back around / Rhythm runs on a tala, a cycle of a fixed number of beats that repeats through the performance. A favorite in the north is tintal: 16 beats in four groups of four, which musicians track with claps and waves of the hand. The first beat, the sam, is the point of greatest rhythmic resolution. Drummer and soloist love patterns that pull against the cycle, and then they land together back on sam.

### ☐ `fact.music.half_string_octave`: unverified

> **Claim:** At the same tension, a string half as long vibrates twice as fast, so the 2:1 length ratio sounds an octave higher.

- **Concept:** Pythagoras and musical ratios (`concept.music.pythagorean_ratios`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L22 “Music in Ancient Greece” · `card.music.022.c1` (text): Pluck a string, then pluck half of it. Same note, only higher. / At the same tension, the half-length string vibrates twice as fast, and you hear the octave. Greek tradition says Pythagoras found the numbers hiding behind sounds like this. Then Greek thinkers went further and argued that music could shape who you become.
  - L22 “Music in Ancient Greece” · `card.music.022.c2` (text): Harmony by the numbers / Greek tradition credits Pythagoras, a 6th-century-BCE philosopher, with finding that the sweetest intervals match simple ratios of string length. Halve a string (2:1) and you get the octave. Take two-thirds of it (3:2) for a fifth, three-quarters (4:3) for a fourth. Remember Level 8's A climbing from 440 to 880 Hz? That's the same 2:1, seen from the frequency side: half the length, double the vibrations.
- **Tested by:**
  - L22 `question.music.022.q1`: In the Greek ratios credited to Pythagoras, which string-length ratio gives the octave? → **2:1**

### ☐ `fact.music.instruments_bow_stick_slip`: unverified

> **Claim:** A rosined bow grips the string and drags it sideways until the string slips back; this stick-slip cycle repeats once per vibration, keeping the note going.

- **Concept:** Bows and bodies (`concept.music.instruments_string_sound`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L12 “Strings” · `card.music.012.c4` (text): The bow: grab, drag, slip / A bow keeps a string going. Its hair is rubbed with sticky rosin, so it grips the string and drags it sideways until the string snaps free and slides back. Then it catches again. This grab and slip repeats once for every vibration, feeding the string energy the whole time, which is why a bowed note can last as long as the bow does.
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Euphonics (Jim Woodhouse, Cambridge) and bowed-string research describe the string sticking to the rosined bow, then slipping back, repeating at the string's frequency (Helmholtz motion). Sources: https://euphonics.org/9-6-friction-and-rosin-a-sticky-problem/, https://euphonics.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/BowedStringReview.pdf

> **Claim:** On an acoustic guitar, the strings barely sound on their own; the bridge and saddle pass their vibration to the top plate, which radiates the sound.

- **Appears in:**
  - L17 “The Guitar” · `card.music.017.c2` (text): How a guitar makes its notes / Level 12 applies here too. The strings barely sound on their own, so the bridge and saddle pass their vibration into the guitar's top plate, which moves the air. To change notes, you press a string against a fret, one of the note markers across the neck. That shortens the part that vibrates, and a shorter string sounds higher.
  - L17 “The Guitar” · `card.music.017.c4` (text): One recipe, many branches / Wherever the guitar went, new relatives grew. Latin America has its own small guitars, like the Mexican jarana and the South American charango. In Hawaii, the Portuguese machete became the ukulele. Sizes, string counts and names change, but the recipe holds: strings shortened against a neck, and a hollow body to make them loud.
- **Tested by:**
  - L17 `question.music.017.q2`: What does pressing a guitar string against a fret do? → **Shortens the vibrating part, raising the note**

- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Wikipedia (Bridge (instrument)) says the bridge transfers string vibration to the soundboard, which moves far more air than the strings. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bridge_(instrument)

### ☐ `fact.music.instruments_string_pitch_factors`: unverified

> **Claim:** A string sounds higher when it is shorter, tighter or lighter, and lower when it is longer, looser or heavier (thicker).

- **Concept:** How a string sets its note (`concept.music.instruments_string_pitch`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L12 “Strings” · `card.music.012.c2` (text): Three ways to change a string's note / A string sounds higher when it's shorter, tighter or lighter, and lower when it's longer, looser or heavier. Players use all three. Tighten a string and it rises. Press a finger down and you shorten the part that vibrates, so the note climbs. And the low strings are the thick ones: the extra weight drags their notes down.
  - L15 “Percussion” · `card.music.015.c4` (text): Tuning a drum / A drumhead behaves a lot like Level 12's string: the tighter it's stretched, the higher it sounds. Timpani, the big kettledrums, use this to hit exact notes, and they're the only drums in a Western orchestra tuned to definite pitch. By the 16th century, screws around their copper shells tightened the heads. They're usually played in pairs, tuned to different pitches.
  - L17 “The Guitar” · `card.music.017.c2` (text): How a guitar makes its notes / Level 12 applies here too. The strings barely sound on their own, so the bridge and saddle pass their vibration into the guitar's top plate, which moves the air. To change notes, you press a string against a fret, one of the note markers across the neck. That shortens the part that vibrates, and a shorter string sounds higher.
- **Tested by:**
  - L12 `question.music.012.q1`: Which change to a string makes its note sound higher? → **Making it shorter**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. SchoolPhysics and the Understanding Sound textbook give f = (1/2L)(T/mu)^(1/2): shorter length, higher tension or lower mass per length raises the frequency. Sources: https://www.schoolphysics.co.uk/age16-19/Sound/text/Vibrating_strings/index.html, https://pressbooks.pub/sound/chapter/vibrating-strings/

Fewer than 300 melodies do. / The songs, by some 450 troubadours, were copied into songbooks called chansonniers, but most were saved without their tunes. So for the great majority, we can read the poem and only guess how it sounded. Remember Level 25: a melody that isn't written down lasts only as long as someone remembers it.

Writing it down let melodies outlast their singers, and Guido's staff let people read tunes they'd never heard. Troubadours show the cost of not writing: most of their melodies are gone. Then voices multiplied, from one line of chant to Pérotin's four, and printing, from Venice in 1501, took polyphony off the scribe's desk.

> **Claim:** Pelog has seven pitches per octave with clearly narrow and wide intervals, but pieces are built on sets of five of those pitches.

Pelog has seven pitches per octave, with clearly narrow and wide steps, but each piece is built on a set of five of them. Music had a primary role in the plays of Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides: a chorus of up to 15 men sang and danced, and an aulos player supplied the music.
